Equality in the Bosonic Quantum Entropy Power Inequality

Yonglong Li Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Statistics Affiliation: Xi’an Jiaotong University Email: liyonglong@xjtu.edu.cn
Abstract

The bosonic quantum entropy power inequality bounds the entropy of a beam-splitter output in terms of the input entropies. We determine its complete equality class among independent inputs of finite mean photon number: for any number of modes and any transmissivity strictly between zero and one, equality in either the linear or the exponential form holds if and only if the inputs are Gaussian with the same covariance matrix, allowing arbitrary displacements. The main step shows that equality for one output forces the two outputs to be independent: a thermal auxiliary converts equality into preservation of mutual information by a fixed noisy channel, and a two-outcome instrument shows that preservation of mutual information requires a product state with the reference. The quantum Darmois–Skitovich theorem then gives Gaussianity, while a central-limit argument reduces exponential equality to linear equality.

Keywords: Quantum entropy power inequality, Gaussian states, beam splitter, mutual information, equality conditions.

1 Introduction

Consider two independent mm-mode bosonic systems, AA and BB, mixed on a beam splitter of transmissivity 0<η<10<\eta<1. If RXR_{X} denotes the vector of position and momentum quadratures of system XX, the outputs are

RC\displaystyle R_{C} =η​RA+1−η​RB,\displaystyle=\sqrt{\eta}R_{A}+\sqrt{1-\eta}R_{B},
RE\displaystyle R_{E} =−1−η​RA+η​RB.\displaystyle=-\sqrt{1-\eta}R_{A}+\sqrt{\eta}R_{B}. (1)

The quantum entropy power inequality (qEPI) lower-bounds the entropy of the retained output CC:

S⁡(C)\displaystyle S(C) ≥η​S​(A)+(1−η)​S​(B),\displaystyle\geq\eta S(A)+(1-\eta)S(B), (2)
eS⁡(C)/m\displaystyle e^{S(C)/m} ≥η​eS⁡(A)/m+(1−η)​eS⁡(B)/m.\displaystyle\geq\eta e^{S(A)/m}+(1-\eta)e^{S(B)/m}. (3)

Here SS is the von Neumann entropy, with natural logarithms. We ask: which independent inputs make either bound exact?

König and Smith [1, 2] proved (2) for every transmissivity and (3) for a balanced beam splitter. De Palma, Mari, and Giovannetti [3] proved the exponential inequality for every transmissivity. The extension to several independent inputs under general linear mixing is due to De Palma, Mari, Lloyd, and Giovannetti [4]. These results provide the inequalities but not a complete finite-energy equality characterization. De Palma et al. observed that Gaussian inputs with proportional covariance matrices fail to attain the exponential bound unless their entropies agree [3, discussion following Eq. (5)]. We establish the complete characterization here.

Equality questions distinguish this quantum problem from its classical counterpart. For independent random vectors with finite covariance matrices and finite differential entropies, equality in the classical EPI of Shannon and Stam [5, 6] characterizes Gaussian inputs with proportional covariances. The linear-entropy form requires identical covariances [7, Sec. II-E1]. In the quantum problem, both forms require identical covariance matrices.

1.1 Main results

Finite energy means finite expectation of total photon number. It guarantees finite covariance matrices and finite input and output entropies. Let UηU_{\eta} denote the beam-splitter unitary in (1).

Theorem 1 (Linear equality).

Let ρA,ρB\rho_{A},\rho_{B} be independent finite-energy mm-mode states, where m≥1m\geq 1 and 0<η<10<\eta<1, and set ωC​E=Uη​(ρA⊗ρB)​Uη†\omega_{CE}=U_{\eta}(\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B})U_{\eta}^{\dagger}. The following statements are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    S⁡(C)=η​S​(A)+(1−η)​S​(B)S(C)=\eta S(A)+(1-\eta)S(B);

  2. (ii)

    ωC​E=ωC⊗ωE\omega_{CE}=\omega_{C}\otimes\omega_{E};

  3. (iii)

    ρA,ρB\rho_{A},\rho_{B} are Gaussian states with the same covariance matrix.

The input displacement vectors may differ.

The equivalence between product outputs and Gaussian inputs is the quantum Darmois–Skitovich characterization [8, Theorem 7, Corollary 8], with a one-mode predecessor in [9]. The new implication is (i)⇒\Rightarrow(ii). It applies to arbitrary mixed inputs and includes Gaussian states with symplectic eigenvalues equal to 1/21/2.

Theorem 2 (Exponential equality).

Let ρA,ρB\rho_{A},\rho_{B} be independent finite-energy mm-mode states, where m≥1m\geq 1 and 0<η<10<\eta<1. For the retained beam-splitter output CC,

eS⁡(C)/m=η​eS⁡(A)/m+(1−η)​eS⁡(B)/me^{S(C)/m}=\eta e^{S(A)/m}+(1-\eta)e^{S(B)/m}

if and only if the inputs are Gaussian with the same covariance matrix, allowing arbitrary displacements.

Thus the two qEPIs have the same equality class. In particular, when both input covariance matrices are fixed to the same matrix, the centered Gaussian pair uniquely minimizes the linear deficit (Corollary 9). For unequal input entropies the qEPI bound is strict at every finite-energy input pair.

This equality question is distinct from the entropy photon-number inequality (EPnI) [10], which asks whether product thermal inputs minimize output entropy for prescribed input entropies. The EPnI is a stronger conjectured bound; see [11, Secs. V.2 and VII.1]. Identical thermal inputs attain the qEPI, whereas thermal inputs with unequal entropies give a strict inequality.

1.2 A first calculation: the two output deficits

The following identity makes the missing implication precise. Define

LC\displaystyle L_{C} =S⁡(C)−η​S​(A)−(1−η)​S​(B),\displaystyle=S(C)-\eta S(A)-(1-\eta)S(B),
LE\displaystyle L_{E} =S⁡(E)−(1−η)​S​(A)−η​S​(B).\displaystyle=S(E)-(1-\eta)S(A)-\eta S(B). (4)

Both quantities are nonnegative. For EE, apply the linear qEPI after the parity transformation RA↦−RAR_{A}\mapsto-R_{A}, which preserves entropy. Since the input is a product and the beam splitter is unitary,

I​(C,E)ω\displaystyle I(C;E)_{\omega} =S⁡(C)+S⁡(E)−S⁡(C​E)\displaystyle=S(C)+S(E)-S(CE)
=S⁡(C)+S⁡(E)−S⁡(A)−S⁡(B)\displaystyle=S(C)+S(E)-S(A)-S(B)
=LC+LE.\displaystyle=L_{C}+L_{E}. (5)

Consequently, product outputs force both deficits to vanish. Theorem 1 proves the converse: LC=0L_{C}=0 already forces LE=0L_{E}=0. Exchanging the roles of the two outputs (transmissivity 1−η1-\eta together with the parity map on AA), the same theorem shows that LE=0L_{E}=0 forces LC=0L_{C}=0.

For pure inputs this implication is immediate. The equality LC=0L_{C}=0 becomes S⁡(C)=0S(C)=0, so the CC marginal is pure and the joint output is a product. The difficulty is to obtain the same conclusion when both input states may be mixed.

1.3 Related work and the proof idea

For identical copies at η=1/2\eta=1/2, Bu and Li [12, Theorems 5 and 7] characterize Gaussianity by product outputs. In the finite-energy class, their criterion is equivalently S⁡(C)+S⁡(E)=2​S​(ρ)S(C)+S(E)=2S(\rho). They also give a pure-state criterion [12, Theorem 1]. Hahn and Takagi [13, Theorem 1] construct a faithful non-Gaussianity measure from the correlations generated by identical-copy mixing. Our starting condition involves a single output, and permits distinct mixed inputs and any nontrivial transmissivity. For discrete-variable systems, Bu, Gu, and Jaffe [14] characterized the minimum-output-entropy inputs of a qudit convolution as pure stabilizer states; the present paper concerns the bosonic equality problem.

The proof uses a doubling construction, an approach familiar from classical Gaussian extremality [15]. Classical arguments combine the entropy chain rule with conditioning on random variables. In the quantum circuit, the corresponding entropy decomposition gives a vanishing conditional mutual information. This alone does not imply unconditional independence. Furthermore, a quantum memory cannot generally be replaced by a family of classical conditional input distributions without changing the state.

Our choice of auxiliary inputs resolves this particular obstruction. We adjoin two identical thermal states and evaluate the doubled circuit in two orders; see Fig. 1. One order gives the entropy decomposition. In the other, the thermal pair supplies independent noise on the two original outputs. The zero conditional mutual information then states that one local noisy channel loses no mutual information.

The channel can prepare a fixed vacuum output with an input-dependent probability. We expose that event with a two-outcome quantum instrument. In the vacuum branch, every correlation with a reference is discarded. If the channel loses no mutual information, the filtered input in that branch must already be a product. The filter is injective, so the original input must be a product as well. An injectivity argument on the other local channel then yields independence of the original beam-splitter outputs.

The inequality used in the doubling step is the conditional qEPI. König [16] proved a conditional linear inequality at weight p=ηp=\eta for two independent Gaussian input–memory pairs, and conjectured a general conditional inequality. De Palma and Trevisan [17] established the conditional qEPI under conditional independence. Their Gaussian construction asymptotically attains the bound for prescribed limiting conditional entropies [17, Theorem 7]. Our unconditional equality classification is obtained from the noisy-channel argument.

For exponential equality, we keep one affine weight fixed under repeated convolution. The doubling identity preserves zero deficit at each iteration. The quantum central limit theorem [18, 19] and entropy continuity [20] then yield Gaussian equality. Strictness within the Gaussian family reduces the question to Theorem 1.

In Section 2 we state our conventions and the conditional qEPI. In Section 3 we develop the two tools and prove linear equality. In Section 4 we prove exponential equality. In Section 5 we discuss further questions. The appendices contain the auxiliary operator calculations and a self-contained finite-energy Darmois–Skitovich proof.

2 Conventions and the conditional qEPI

2.1 Bosonic systems and entropy

We use the standard bosonic framework [21, 22]. An mm-mode system has Hilbert space ℋm=ℓ2​(ℕ0m)\mathcal{H}_{m}=\ell^{2}(\mathbb{N}_{0}^{m}), number basis |𝒏⟩|\bm{n}\rangle, annihilation operators aja_{j}, and quadratures

Qj=aj+aj†2,Pj=aj−aj†i​2.Q_{j}=\frac{a_{j}+a_{j}^{\dagger}}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad P_{j}=\frac{a_{j}-a_{j}^{\dagger}}{i\sqrt{2}}.

Write

R=(Q1,P1,…,Qm,Pm)T,Ω=⨁j=1m(01−10).R=(Q_{1},P_{1},\ldots,Q_{m},P_{m})^{T},\qquad\Omega=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{m}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}.

Then [Rj,Rk]=i​Ωj​k​I[R_{j},R_{k}]=i\Omega_{jk}I, where Ω\Omega is the symplectic form, with ℏ=1\hbar=1 and vacuum covariance I/2I/2.

A state is a positive trace-class operator of trace one. We write ρX=TrY⁡ρX​Y\rho_{X}=\operatorname{Tr}_{Y}\rho_{XY} for a marginal and ‖T‖1=Tr⁡T†​T\left\lVert T\right\rVert_{1}=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{T^{\dagger}T} for trace norm. A channel is a completely positive trace-preserving map on trace-class operators; id\operatorname{id} denotes the identity channel. The total photon-number operator is

Hm=∑j=1maj†​aj=12​RT​R−m2​I.H_{m}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}^{\dagger}a_{j}=\frac{1}{2}R^{T}R-\frac{m}{2}I. (6)

For a finite-energy state ρ\rho, its mean vector dρd_{\rho} and covariance matrix VρV_{\rho} are

dρ\displaystyle d_{\rho} =Tr⁡ρ​R,\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}\rho R,
(Vρ)j​k\displaystyle(V_{\rho})_{jk} =12​Tr⁡ρ⁡{Rj−(dρ)j​I,Rk−(dρ)k​I},\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}\rho\{R_{j}-(d_{\rho})_{j}I,R_{k}-(d_{\rho})_{k}I\}, (7)

where (dρ)k(d_{\rho})_{k} is the kk-th element of the vector dρd_{\rho} and {X,Y}=X​Y+Y​X\{X,Y\}=XY+YX is the anticommutator of operators XX and YY. Unbounded products are interpreted as quadratic-form expectations; details are in Appendix A. A state is centered if dρ=0d_{\rho}=0, and

Tr⁡ρ​Hm=tr⁡Vρ+|dρ|2−m2.\operatorname{Tr}\rho H_{m}=\frac{\operatorname{tr}V_{\rho}+|d_{\rho}|^{2}-m}{2}. (8)

By (8), finite energy is the same as finite second moments of the quadratures, the hypothesis used in the quantum central limit theorem [19, 23].

All logarithms are natural. The von Neumann entropy of a state ρ\rho is S⁡(ρ)=−Tr⁡ρ​log⁡ρS(\rho)=-\operatorname{Tr}\rho\log\rho, with the convention that 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0. Define

g⁡(x)=(x+1)​log⁡(x+1)−x​log⁡x,x≥0.g(x)=(x+1)\log(x+1)-x\log x,\qquad x\geq 0.

The oscillator Gibbs bound [20, 21] is

Tr⁡ρ​Hm≤𝖤⟹S⁡(ρ)≤m​g​(𝖤/m)<∞.\operatorname{Tr}\rho H_{m}\leq\mathsf{E}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad S(\rho)\leq mg(\mathsf{E}/m)<\infty. (9)

Each marginal of a finite-mode, finite-energy state has finite entropy. All beam splitters below preserve total photon number, so this bound applies throughout the circuits.

For finite entropies, our conventions for mutual information, conditional entropy, and conditional mutual information (CMI) are

I⁡(X,Y)\displaystyle I(X;Y) =S⁡(X)+S⁡(Y)−S⁡(X​Y),\displaystyle=S(X)+S(Y)-S(XY),
S⁡(X∣M)\displaystyle S(X\mid M) =S⁡(X​M)−S⁡(M),\displaystyle=S(XM)-S(M), (10)
I⁡(X;Y∣M)\displaystyle I(X;Y\mid M) =S⁡(X∣M)−S⁡(X∣Y​M).\displaystyle=S(X\mid M)-S(X\mid YM). (11)

In general I(X;Y)=D(ρX​Y∥ρX⊗ρY)I(X;Y)=D(\rho_{XY}\|\rho_{X}\otimes\rho_{Y}), where D(ρ∥σ)=Trρ(logρ−logσ)D(\rho\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}\rho(\log\rho-\log\sigma) is the quantum relative entropy [24], which is nonnegative and vanishes if and only if ρ=σ\rho=\sigma; in particular I⁡(X,Y)=0I(X;Y)=0 exactly for product states. We use data processing [24, 25], strong subadditivity [26], and the chain rule I⁡(X​Y,K)=I⁡(X,K)+I⁡(Y;K∣X)I(XY;K)=I(X;K)+I(Y;K\mid X).

2.2 Characteristic functions and Gaussian states

The real Weyl characteristic function is

W⁡(ξ)=ei​ξT​R,χρ​(ξ)=Tr⁡ρ​W​(ξ),ξ∈ℝ2​m.W(\xi)=e^{i\xi^{T}R},\qquad\chi_{\rho}(\xi)=\operatorname{Tr}\rho W(\xi),\qquad\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2m}.

It determines the state. Gaussian states are precisely those for which

χρ​(ξ)=exp⁡(i​dT​ξ−12​ξT​V​ξ).\chi_{\rho}(\xi)=\exp(id^{T}\xi-\tfrac{1}{2}\xi^{T}V\xi). (12)

A real symmetric matrix VV is the covariance matrix of some quantum state if and only if V+i​Ω/2≥0V+i\Omega/2\geq 0 [22]. Write γV\gamma_{V} for the unique centered Gaussian state with covariance VV. Its Williamson form and entropy are

V\displaystyle V =𝖲​diag⁡(ν1,ν1,…,νm,νm)​𝖲T,\displaystyle=\mathsf{S}\operatorname{diag}(\nu_{1},\nu_{1},\ldots,\nu_{m},\nu_{m})\mathsf{S}^{T},
𝖲​Ω​𝖲T=Ω,νj≥12,\displaystyle\hskip 42.67912pt\mathsf{S}\Omega\mathsf{S}^{T}=\Omega,\quad\nu_{j}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}, (13)
S⁡(γV)\displaystyle S(\gamma_{V}) =∑j=1mg⁡(νj−12).\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}g(\nu_{j}-\tfrac{1}{2}). (14)

𝒟⁡(z)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}(z) =exp⁡(∑jzj​aj†−z¯j​aj),\displaystyle=\exp\!\left(\sum_{j}z_{j}a_{j}^{\dagger}-\bar{z}_{j}a_{j}\right), ρ^​(z)\displaystyle\widehat{\rho}(z) =Tr⁡ρ​𝒟​(z),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}\rho\mathcal{D}(z), (15)
W⁡(ξ)\displaystyle W(\xi) =𝒟⁡(z⁡(ξ)),\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}(z(\xi)), z​(ξ)j\displaystyle z(\xi)_{j} =−ξ2​j+i​ξ2​j−12.\displaystyle=\frac{-\xi_{2j}+i\xi_{2j-1}}{\sqrt{2}}. (16)

Here z∈ℂmz\in\mathbb{C}^{m}, and |z⟩=𝒟⁡(z)​|0⟩|z\rangle=\mathcal{D}(z)|0\rangle is a coherent state. Displacement changes the mean and preserves covariance and entropy. After matching quadrature ordering, De Palma–Trevisan’s real argument is related to ours by ξ=Ω​x\xi=\Omega x; Cuesta’s is related by ξ=−Ω​x\xi=-\Omega x, and his covariance is Γ=2​V\Gamma=2V.11 1 Theorem and equation numbers in citations refer to the arXiv versions of the cited works; their identifiers are given in the bibliography.

The retained beam-splitter channel is

ℬη​(TA​B)=TrE⁡(Uη​TA​B​Uη†).\mathcal{B}_{\eta}(T_{AB})=\operatorname{Tr}_{E}(U_{\eta}T_{AB}U_{\eta}^{\dagger}). (17)

χC​E​(u,v)=\displaystyle\chi_{CE}(u,v)={} χA​(η​u−1−η​v)​χB​(1−η​u+η​v).\displaystyle\chi_{A}(\sqrt{\eta}\,u-\sqrt{1-\eta}\,v)\chi_{B}(\sqrt{1-\eta}\,u+\sqrt{\eta}\,v). (18)

2.3 The affine deficit

The proof uses a variational weight pp, distinct from the physical transmissivity η\eta. For 0≤p≤10\leq p\leq 1 and 0<q<10<q<1, let

d(p∥q)=plogpq+(1−p)log1−p1−q.d(p\|q)=p\log\frac{p}{q}+(1-p)\log\frac{1-p}{1-q}. (19)

For independent inputs define

Fp​(A,B)\displaystyle F_{p}(A,B) =S(C)−pS(A)−(1−p)S(B)+md(p∥η),\displaystyle=S(C)-pS(A)-(1-p)S(B)+md(p\|\eta), (20)

For a joint state ρA​B​M\rho_{ABM}, with ρC​M=(ℬη⊗idM)​(ρA​B​M)\rho_{CM}=(\mathcal{B}_{\eta}\otimes\operatorname{id}_{M})(\rho_{ABM}), define

Fp​(A,B∣M)=\displaystyle F_{p}(A,B\mid M)={} S(C∣M)−pS(A∣M)−(1−p)S(B∣M)+md(p∥η).\displaystyle S(C\mid M)-pS(A\mid M)-(1-p)S(B\mid M)+md(p\|\eta). (22)

I⁡(A;B∣M)=0⟹Fp​(A,B∣M)≥0I(A;B\mid M)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F_{p}(A,B\mid M)\geq 0 (23)

for every p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1], provided the bosonic inputs have finite energy and S⁡(M)<∞S(M)<\infty. A one-dimensional memory gives the unconditional inequality. Below the memory consists of finite-energy bosonic modes.

3 Proof of linear equality

We first establish an entropy decomposition and a strict information-loss property. Their combination will prove Theorem 1.

3.1 Conditional doubling

Start with four independent finite-energy mm-mode input systems in the state

ρA1⊗ρB1⊗ρA2⊗ρB2.\rho_{A_{1}}\otimes\rho_{B_{1}}\otimes\rho_{A_{2}}\otimes\rho_{B_{2}}. (24)

The two pairs may be different. Mix A1,A2A_{1},A_{2} on a balanced beam splitter, and independently mix B1,B2B_{1},B_{2} in the same way:

RA+=RA1+RA22,RA−=−RA1+RA22,R_{A_{+}}=\frac{R_{A_{1}}+R_{A_{2}}}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad R_{A_{-}}=\frac{-R_{A_{1}}+R_{A_{2}}}{\sqrt{2}}, (25)

with analogous definitions for BB. We call these two balanced beam splitters the copy step. Then apply the η\eta-beam splitter UηU_{\eta} to A+​B+A_{+}B_{+} and to A−​B−A_{-}B_{-}, producing C+​E+C_{+}E_{+} and C−​E−C_{-}E_{-}. Set M=A+​B+M=A_{+}B_{+} before converting it unitarily to C+​E+C_{+}E_{+}. To specify the states underlying these labels, write ζ\zeta for the state after the copy step:

ζA+​A−​B+​B−=\displaystyle\zeta_{A_{+}A_{-}B_{+}B_{-}}={} [U1/2​(ρA1⊗ρA2)​U1/2†]⊗[U1/2​(ρB1⊗ρB2)​U1/2†].\displaystyle\bigl[U_{1/2}(\rho_{A_{1}}\otimes\rho_{A_{2}})U_{1/2}^{\dagger}\bigr]\otimes\bigl[U_{1/2}(\rho_{B_{1}}\otimes\rho_{B_{2}})U_{1/2}^{\dagger}\bigr]. (26)

Tensor factors are reordered according to their labels. Applying ℬη\mathcal{B}_{\eta} to the minus pair and retaining MM gives a state on C−​MC_{-}M. Applying the η\eta-beam splitter to MM then gives the same state on C−​C+​E+C_{-}C_{+}E_{+}. The latter is a marginal of the four-output state, denoted ΞC+​E+​C−​E−\Xi_{C_{+}E_{+}C_{-}E_{-}}. The labels MM and C+​E+C_{+}E_{+} describe the memory before and after its η\eta-beam splitter, respectively.

This construction is a quantum version of the doubling trick used in classical Gaussian extremality arguments [15]. Here the conditional qEPI provides the nonnegative remainder. Mixing two input pairs separates their total deficit into the deficit of the plus pair, the deficit of the minus pair conditioned on the plus inputs, and a correlation term. The following identity makes all three terms nonnegative. Allowing the two input pairs to differ will let us choose a thermal auxiliary in Section 3.4.

Lemma 3 (Doubling with different pairs).

Let ζA−​B−​M\zeta_{A_{-}B_{-}M} be the state in (26), with tensor factors reordered and M=A+​B+M=A_{+}B_{+}. Define

ζC−​M=(ℬη⊗idM)​(ζA−​B−​M).\zeta_{C_{-}M}=(\mathcal{B}_{\eta}\otimes\operatorname{id}_{M})(\zeta_{A_{-}B_{-}M}).

The conditional deficit below uses these two states; the CMI is evaluated in the four-output state Ξ\Xi. For each fixed p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1],

Fp​(A1,B1)+Fp​(A2,B2)=Fp​(A+,B+)+Fp​(A−,B−∣M)+I⁡(C−;E+∣C+).\displaystyle F_{p}(A_{1},B_{1})+F_{p}(A_{2},B_{2})=F_{p}(A_{+},B_{+})+F_{p}(A_{-},B_{-}\mid M)+I(C_{-};E_{+}\mid C_{+}). (27)

All three terms on the right are nonnegative.

Proof.

The product in (26) proves independence between the entire AA-group and the entire BB-group. Indeed,

S⁡(A−∣A+​B+)=S⁡(A−​A+)+S⁡(B+)−S⁡(A+)−S⁡(B+)=S⁡(A−∣A+).\displaystyle S(A_{-}\mid A_{+}B_{+})=S(A_{-}A_{+})+S(B_{+})-S(A_{+})-S(B_{+})=S(A_{-}\mid A_{+}). (28)

Similarly S⁡(B−∣A+​B+)=S⁡(B−∣B+)S(B_{-}\mid A_{+}B_{+})=S(B_{-}\mid B_{+}). Moreover

S⁡(A−​B−∣A+​B+)=S⁡(A−∣A+)+S⁡(B−∣B+),S(A_{-}B_{-}\mid A_{+}B_{+})=S(A_{-}\mid A_{+})+S(B_{-}\mid B_{+}), (29)

which verifies conditional independence explicitly. Hence

I⁡(A−;B−∣A+​B+)\displaystyle I(A_{-};B_{-}\mid A_{+}B_{+}) =0,\displaystyle=0,
S⁡(A−∣M)\displaystyle S(A_{-}\mid M) =S⁡(A−∣A+),\displaystyle=S(A_{-}\mid A_{+}),
S⁡(B−∣M)\displaystyle S(B_{-}\mid M) =S⁡(B−∣B+).\displaystyle=S(B_{-}\mid B_{+}). (30)

The AA entropy terms in the right side of (27) satisfy

S⁡(A+)+S⁡(A−∣M)\displaystyle S(A_{+})+S(A_{-}\mid M) =S⁡(A+​A−)\displaystyle=S(A_{+}A_{-})
=S⁡(A1​A2)=S⁡(A1)+S⁡(A2),\displaystyle=S(A_{1}A_{2})=S(A_{1})+S(A_{2}), (31)

where the final equality uses independence of the original inputs. Multiplication by −p-p gives the desired AA contribution; the BB argument is identical with coefficient −(1−p)-(1-p). The output terms combine as

S⁡(C+)+S⁡(C−∣M)+I⁡(C−;E+∣C+)\displaystyle S(C_{+})+S(C_{-}\mid M)+I(C_{-};E_{+}\mid C_{+})
=S⁡(C+)+S⁡(C−∣C+)\displaystyle\qquad=S(C_{+})+S(C_{-}\mid C_{+})
=S⁡(C+​C−).\displaystyle\qquad=S(C_{+}C_{-}). (32)

The equality of the two conditional entropies follows by applying the η\eta-beam splitter to the memory in both entropy terms:

S​(C−∣M)ζ\displaystyle S(C_{-}\mid M)_{\zeta} =S​(C−​M)ζ−S​(M)ζ\displaystyle=S(C_{-}M)_{\zeta}-S(M)_{\zeta}
=S​(C−​C+​E+)Ξ−S​(C+​E+)Ξ\displaystyle=S(C_{-}C_{+}E_{+})_{\Xi}-S(C_{+}E_{+})_{\Xi}
=S​(C−∣C+​E+)Ξ.\displaystyle=S(C_{-}\mid C_{+}E_{+})_{\Xi}. (33)

The copy step commutes with the η\eta-beam splitters: the former acts on the pair index and the latter on the A/BA/B index. To check this directly, put a=ηa=\sqrt{\eta}, b=1−ηb=\sqrt{1-\eta} and first define RCi=a​RAi+b​RBiR_{C_{i}}=aR_{A_{i}}+bR_{B_{i}} and REi=−b​RAi+a​RBiR_{E_{i}}=-bR_{A_{i}}+aR_{B_{i}} for i=1,2i=1,2. Substitution shows

RC+=RC1+RC22,RC−=−RC1+RC22,R_{C_{+}}=\frac{R_{C_{1}}+R_{C_{2}}}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad R_{C_{-}}=\frac{-R_{C_{1}}+R_{C_{2}}}{\sqrt{2}}, (34)

with the same identities for E+,E−E_{+},E_{-}. Both circuit orderings therefore have the same action on all Weyl operators and the same joint output state. If the η\eta-beam splitters act first, C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} are independent and the copy step acts unitarily on them. Therefore S⁡(C+​C−)=S⁡(C1)+S⁡(C2)S(C_{+}C_{-})=S(C_{1})+S(C_{2}). The two constant terms on the right are 2md(p∥η)2m\,d(p\|\eta), proving the identity.

Since all initial energies are finite and passive beam splitters preserve total energy, every joint entropy here is finite. The first term is nonnegative by unconditional affine qEPI, the second by conditional affine qEPI and (30), and the third by strong subadditivity. ∎

The consequence needed for linear equality is obtained by setting p=ηp=\eta:

Lη​(A1,B1)=Lη​(A2,B2)=0\displaystyle L_{\eta}(A_{1},B_{1})=L_{\eta}(A_{2},B_{2})=0 (35)
⟹I⁡(C−;E+∣C+)=0.\displaystyle{}\Longrightarrow I(C_{-};E_{+}\mid C_{+})=0.

3.2 A thermal channel with a common vacuum component

For N>0N>0, define the mm-mode product thermal state with mean photon number NN per mode by

τN=⨂j=1m[1N+1​∑n=0∞(NN+1)n​|n⟩​⟨n|].\tau_{N}=\bigotimes_{j=1}^{m}\left[\frac{1}{N+1}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{N}{N+1}\right)^{n}|n\rangle\!\langle n|\right]. (36)

Set τ0=|0⟩​⟨0|\tau_{0}=|0\rangle\!\langle 0| when N=0N=0. Its covariance is (N+12)​I2​m(N+\frac{1}{2})I_{2m}. Fix once and for all the channel

Φ⁡(ρ)=ℬ1/2​(ρ⊗τ2).\Phi(\rho)=\mathcal{B}_{1/2}(\rho\otimes\tau_{2}). (37)

This is the thermal attenuator of transmissivity 1/21/2 with environment τ2\tau_{2}. The environment energy N=2N=2 makes it a measure-and-prepare channel: a heterodyne measurement followed by preparation of a displaced τ1/2\tau_{1/2} state. Such a channel is entanglement breaking: when applied to one part of a joint state, its output is a mixture of product states. We use the more specific fact that every prepared state contains a component along the vacuum. Any bath mean photon number N>1N>1 gives a similar representation, with prepared thermal mean (N−1)/2>0(N-1)/2>0. The choice N=2N=2 keeps the constants simple. The transmissivity of Φ\Phi is 1/21/2, independent of the physical η\eta.

3.2.1 Measure-and-prepare representation

For z∈ℂmz\in\mathbb{C}^{m}, the coherent state is

|z⟩=𝒟(z)|0⟩=e−|z|2/2∑𝒏∈ℕ0mz1n1⋯zmnmn1!⋯nm!|𝒏⟩.|z\rangle=\mathcal{D}(z)|0\rangle=e^{-|z|^{2}/2}\sum_{\bm{n}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{m}}\frac{z_{1}^{n_{1}}\cdots z_{m}^{n_{m}}}{\sqrt{n_{1}!\cdots n_{m}!}}|\bm{n}\rangle. (38)

It satisfies ⟨u|v⟩=exp[−(|u|2+|v|2)/2+u¯⋅v]\langle u|v\rangle=\exp[-(|u|^{2}+|v|^{2})/2+\bar{u}\cdot v]. The heterodyne measurement is the positive-operator-valued measure (POVM)

Mhet​(𝑑z)=π−m​|z⟩​⟨z|​d2​m​z,∫ℂmMhet​(𝑑z)=I.M_{\rm het}(\mathrm{d}z)=\pi^{-m}|z\rangle\langle z|\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z,\qquad\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}M_{\rm het}(\mathrm{d}z)=I. (39)

A POVM assigns positive operators to measurable outcome sets and sums to the identity; d2​m​z\mathrm{d}^{2m}z denotes Lebesgue measure in the real and imaginary coordinates of ℂm\mathbb{C}^{m}. The second identity in (39) follows by inserting (38) and integrating its number-basis entries. For a state ρ\rho, the outcome density is its Husimi QQ-function [28],

Qρ​(z)=π−m​⟨z|ρ|z⟩,∫ℂmQρ​(z)​d2​m​z=1.Q_{\rho}(z)=\pi^{-m}\langle z|\rho|z\rangle,\qquad\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}Q_{\rho}(z)\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z=1. (40)

Holevo [29, Theorem 2, Eqs. (30)–(31)] gives the general measure-and-prepare form of entanglement-breaking Gaussian channels. The representation below is the special case for Φ\Phi; the direct verification fixes the environment photon number and the prepared-state noise in our convention.

Lemma 4.

For every input state,

Φ⁡(ρ)\displaystyle\Phi(\rho) =∫ℂmQρ​(z)​πz​d2​m​z,\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}Q_{\rho}(z)\,\pi_{z}\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z,
πz\displaystyle\pi_{z} =𝒟⁡(z/2)​τ1/2​𝒟​(z/2)†.\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}(z/\sqrt{2})\tau_{1/2}\mathcal{D}(z/\sqrt{2})^{\dagger}. (41)
Proof.

Use the complex displacement characteristic function ρ^​(w)=Tr⁡ρ​𝒟​(w)\widehat{\rho}(w)=\operatorname{Tr}\rho\mathcal{D}(w). The heterodyne Fourier identity is

∫Qρ(z)e∑j(wj​z¯j−w¯j​zj)d2​mz=ρ^(w)e−|w|2/2.\int Q_{\rho}(z)e^{\sum_{j}(w_{j}\bar{z}_{j}-\bar{w}_{j}z_{j})}\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z=\widehat{\rho}(w)e^{-|w|^{2}/2}. (42)

The thermal characteristic function is

τN^​(w)=e−(N+1/2)​|w|2,\widehat{\tau_{N}}(w)=e^{-(N+1/2)|w|^{2}},

as follows from its Gaussian covariance (N+1/2)​I(N+1/2)I and (16). For a displaced state,

Tr⁡[𝒟⁡(α)​ρ​𝒟​(α)†​𝒟​(w)]=ew⋅α¯−w¯⋅α​ρ^​(w).\operatorname{Tr}[\mathcal{D}(\alpha)\rho\mathcal{D}(\alpha)^{\dagger}\mathcal{D}(w)]=e^{w\cdot\bar{\alpha}-\bar{w}\cdot\alpha}\widehat{\rho}(w).

Let Φprep\Phi_{\rm prep} denote the integral map on the right of (41). The three factors in its characteristic function are

Φprep​(ρ)^​(w)\displaystyle\widehat{\Phi_{\rm prep}(\rho)}(w) =e−|w|2​∫Qρ​(z)​e(w⋅z¯−w¯⋅z)/2​d2​m​z\displaystyle=e^{-|w|^{2}}\int Q_{\rho}(z)e^{(w\cdot\bar{z}-\bar{w}\cdot z)/\sqrt{2}}\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z
=(a)e−|w|2ρ^(w/2)e−|w|2/4\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{=}e^{-|w|^{2}}\widehat{\rho}(w/\sqrt{2})e^{-|w|^{2}/4}
=ρ^(w/2)e−5|w|2/4.\displaystyle=\widehat{\rho}(w/\sqrt{2})e^{-5|w|^{2}/4}. (43)

Step (a) uses the Fourier identity (42) at w/2w/\sqrt{2}; Appendix A.3 gives its coherent-state verification. On the other hand, the beam-splitter formula gives

Φ⁡(ρ)^(w)=ρ^(w/2)τ2^(w/2)=ρ^(w/2)e−5|w|2/4.\widehat{\Phi(\rho)}(w)=\widehat{\rho}(w/\sqrt{2})\widehat{\tau_{2}}(w/\sqrt{2})=\widehat{\rho}(w/\sqrt{2})e^{-5|w|^{2}/4}. (44)

Uniqueness of characteristic functions proves (41). The integral is in trace norm; its justification is in Appendix A. ∎

3.2.2 The vacuum component

Lemma 5.

Each state in (41) satisfies

πz≥c⁡(z)​|0⟩​⟨0|,c⁡(z)=(23)m​e−|z|2∈(0,1).\pi_{z}\geq c(z)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|,\qquad c(z)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{m}e^{-|z|^{2}}\in(0,1). (45)

Thus πz=c⁡(z)​|0⟩​⟨0|+(1−c⁡(z))​κz\pi_{z}=c(z)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|+(1-c(z))\kappa_{z} for a measurable family of states κz\kappa_{z}.

Proof.

The thermal formula gives τ1/2=(2/3)m​3−Hm\tau_{1/2}=(2/3)^{m}3^{-H_{m}}. With α=z/2\alpha=z/\sqrt{2},

⟨0|πz−1|0⟩\displaystyle\langle 0|\pi_{z}^{-1}|0\rangle =(32)m​⟨−α|3Hm|−α⟩\displaystyle=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{m}\langle-\alpha|3^{H_{m}}|-\alpha\rangle
=(32)m​e2​|α|2=(32)m​e|z|2.\displaystyle=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{m}e^{2|\alpha|^{2}}=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{m}e^{|z|^{2}}. (46)

For one mode the required series is

⟨α|3a†​a|α⟩=e−|α|2​∑n=0∞3n​|α|2​nn!=e2​|α|2;\langle\alpha|3^{a^{\dagger}a}|\alpha\rangle=e^{-|\alpha|^{2}}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{3^{n}|\alpha|^{2n}}{n!}=e^{2|\alpha|^{2}}; (47)

multiplication over the modes proves the middle equality of (46). Each prepared thermal state has zero kernel. The inverse in that equation is interpreted as its quadratic form, namely ‖πz−1/2|0⟩‖2\left\lVert\pi_{z}^{-1/2}|0\rangle\right\rVert^{2}. In particular πz−1/2|0⟩\pi_{z}^{-1/2}|0\rangle is a well-defined Hilbert space vector. For every vector vv, Cauchy–Schwarz gives

|⟨0|v⟩|2=|⟨πz−1/20,πz1/2v⟩|2≤⟨0|πz−1|0⟩⟨v,πzv⟩.|\langle 0|v\rangle|^{2}=|\langle\pi_{z}^{-1/2}0,\pi_{z}^{1/2}v\rangle|^{2}\leq\langle 0|\pi_{z}^{-1}|0\rangle\,\langle v,\pi_{z}v\rangle. (48)

This is the operator inequality (45) with the reciprocal of (46). Define κz=(πz−c⁡(z)​|0⟩​⟨0|)/(1−c⁡(z))\kappa_{z}=(\pi_{z}-c(z)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|)/(1-c(z)). It is positive and has trace one. The map z↦πzz\mapsto\pi_{z} is trace-norm continuous, as follows from strong continuity of displacements acting on a trace-class operator. The function c⁡(z)c(z) is continuous and 1−c⁡(z)≥1−(2/3)m>01-c(z)\geq 1-(2/3)^{m}>0. Thus z↦κzz\mapsto\kappa_{z} is trace-norm continuous, in particular measurable. ∎

3.3 A two-outcome instrument and strict information loss

The vacuum component in Lemma 5 allows us to split Φ\Phi into two branches. In one branch the channel prepares the vacuum and therefore discards all correlations with a reference system. We shall show that this branch has positive probability for every input and that its preceding filter cannot turn a correlated state into a product. These two facts give the required equality criterion.

Integrating the vacuum weight against the heterodyne POVM defines the effect (a positive operator bounded by the identity)

G=∫ℂmc⁡(z)​Mhet​(𝑑z)=3−m​2−Hm,0<G≤3−m​I.G=\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}c(z)M_{\rm het}(\mathrm{d}z)=3^{-m}2^{-H_{m}},\qquad 0<G\leq 3^{-m}I. (49)

Here 0<G0<G means that GG has zero kernel, not that it has a positive uniform lower bound. To check the formula, in one mode insert the coherent-state expansion and integrate in polar coordinates:

1π​∫ℂe−|z|2​|z⟩​⟨z|​d2​z=∑n=0∞2−(n+1)​|n⟩​⟨n|.\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}e^{-|z|^{2}}|z\rangle\langle z|\,\mathrm{d}^{2}z=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}2^{-(n+1)}|n\rangle\langle n|. (50)

Multiplication over the modes and the factor (2/3)m(2/3)^{m} in c⁡(z)c(z) give (49). Equation (50) is the Glauber–Sudarshan PP-representation of the thermal state with one photon per mode [30]; thus G=(2/3)m​τ1G=(2/3)^{m}\tau_{1} is a multiple of a thermal state.

Define two completely positive maps by

Λ1​(ρ)\displaystyle\Lambda_{1}(\rho) =Tr⁡(G​ρ)​|0⟩​⟨0|,\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}(G\rho)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|,
Λ0​(ρ)\displaystyle\Lambda_{0}(\rho) =∫ℂmQρ​(z)​[πz−c⁡(z)​|0⟩​⟨0|]​d2​m​z.\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}Q_{\rho}(z)[\pi_{z}-c(z)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|]\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z. (51)

The kernel in the second integral is positive by Lemma 5; hence it defines a completely positive measure-and-prepare map. Its trace is Tr⁡Λ0​(ρ)=Tr⁡[(I−G)​ρ]\operatorname{Tr}\Lambda_{0}(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}[(I-G)\rho], and Φ=Λ1+Λ0\Phi=\Lambda_{1}+\Lambda_{0}. Complete positivity of the integral maps is verified in Appendix A.4.

For f=0,1f=0,1, let

M1=G1/2,M0=(I−G)1/2,ℐf​(ρ)=Mf​ρ​Mf.M_{1}=G^{1/2},\qquad M_{0}=(I-G)^{1/2},\qquad\mathcal{I}_{f}(\rho)=M_{f}\rho M_{f}. (52)

Since M02+M12=IM_{0}^{2}+M_{1}^{2}=I, the map

ℳ⁡(ρ)=∑f=01|f⟩​⟨f|F⊗ℐf​(ρ)\mathcal{M}(\rho)=\sum_{f=0}^{1}|f\rangle\langle f|_{F}\otimes\mathcal{I}_{f}(\rho) (53)

is a channel. It records a two-valued outcome in the classical register FF and retains the filtered input, denoted X′X^{\prime}. Moreover, I−G≥(1−3−m)​II-G\geq(1-3^{-m})I, so (I−G)−1/2(I-G)^{-1/2} is bounded and

Ψ0(σ)=Λ0((I−G)−1/2σ(I−G)−1/2)\Psi_{0}(\sigma)=\Lambda_{0}\bigl((I-G)^{-1/2}\sigma(I-G)^{-1/2}\bigr) (54)

is a channel: it is completely positive, and its trace is Tr⁡σ\operatorname{Tr}\sigma. After the instrument, replace X′X^{\prime} by the vacuum when F=1F=1 and apply Ψ0\Psi_{0} when F=0F=0. Discarding FF then gives exactly Φ\Phi, since Ψ0∘ℐ0=Λ0\Psi_{0}\circ\mathcal{I}_{0}=\Lambda_{0}.

Proposition 6 (Strict information loss for Φ\Phi).

Let ωX​K\omega_{XK} be a state such that XX consists of m≥1m\geq 1 bosonic modes with Tr⁡(ωX​Hm)<∞\operatorname{Tr}(\omega_{X}H_{m})<\infty, and the reference system KK has a separable Hilbert space with S⁡(ωK)<∞S(\omega_{K})<\infty. Write ζY​K=(Φ⊗idK)​(ωX​K)\zeta_{YK}=(\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{K})(\omega_{XK}). Then

I(X;K)ω=I(Y;K)ζ⟺ωX​K=ωX⊗ωK.I(X;K)_{\omega}=I(Y;K)_{\zeta}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\omega_{XK}=\omega_{X}\otimes\omega_{K}. (55)
Proof.

Let pf=Tr⁡(Mf​ωX​Mf)p_{f}=\operatorname{Tr}(M_{f}\omega_{X}M_{f}). Equation (49) implies p1>0p_{1}>0, because all its number-basis eigenvalues are positive, and p0≥1−3−m>0p_{0}\geq 1-3^{-m}>0. The conditional states after the instrument are

ωX′​Kf=pf−1​(Mf⊗IK)​ωX​K​(Mf⊗IK).\omega^{f}_{X^{\prime}K}=p_{f}^{-1}(M_{f}\otimes I_{K})\omega_{XK}(M_{f}\otimes I_{K}). (56)

Both transformations preserve the corresponding KK marginal. The state with the flag retained is ζF​Y​K=∑fpf​|f⟩​⟨f|F⊗ζY​Kf\zeta_{FYK}=\sum_{f}p_{f}|f\rangle\langle f|_{F}\otimes\zeta^{f}_{YK}.

All branch and joint entropies below are finite, as verified in Appendix A.4. Thus ordinary entropy chain rules apply.

Data processing for ℳ\mathcal{M}, followed by the chain rule for a classical flag, gives

I​(X,K)ω\displaystyle I(X;K)_{\omega} ≥(a)​I​(F​X′,K)(ℳ⊗idK)​(ω)\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{\geq}I(FX^{\prime};K)_{(\mathcal{M}\otimes\operatorname{id}_{K})(\omega)}
=I⁡(F,K)+p1​I​(X′,K)ω1+p0​I​(X′,K)ω0.\displaystyle=I(F;K)+p_{1}I(X^{\prime};K)_{\omega^{1}}+p_{0}I(X^{\prime};K)_{\omega^{0}}. (57)

On the other hand, discarding the flag and then using data processing for Ψ0\Psi_{0} gives

I​(Y,K)ζ\displaystyle I(Y;K)_{\zeta} ≤(b)​I​(F​Y,K)ζ\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(b)}}{\leq}I(FY;K)_{\zeta}

≤(c)​I​(F,K)+p0​I​(X′,K)ω0.\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(c)}}{\leq}I(F;K)+p_{0}I(X^{\prime};K)_{\omega^{0}}. (58)

Steps (a), (b), and (c) apply data processing to the instrument, discarding the flag, and the channel Ψ0\Psi_{0}, respectively. The F​KFK marginal is the same in both displays, and the f=1f=1 term vanishes in the second display because ζ1\zeta^{1} is a product. Subtracting yields

I​(X,K)ω−I​(Y,K)ζ≥p1​I​(X′,K)ω1.I(X;K)_{\omega}-I(Y;K)_{\zeta}\geq p_{1}I(X^{\prime};K)_{\omega^{1}}. (59)

If the left side is zero, then ω1=ωX′1⊗ωK1\omega^{1}=\omega^{1}_{X^{\prime}}\otimes\omega^{1}_{K}. Taking its X′X^{\prime} marginal in (56) therefore gives

(G1/2⊗IK)​ωX​K​(G1/2⊗IK)=(G1/2​ωX​G1/2)⊗ωK1.(G^{1/2}\otimes I_{K})\omega_{XK}(G^{1/2}\otimes I_{K})=(G^{1/2}\omega_{X}G^{1/2})\otimes\omega_{K}^{1}. (60)

For number-basis vectors |𝒏⟩,|𝒏′⟩|\bm{n}\rangle,|\bm{n}^{\prime}\rangle, their eigenvalues g𝒏=3−m2−∑jnjg_{\bm{n}}=3^{-m}2^{-\sum_{j}n_{j}} and g𝒏′g_{\bm{n}^{\prime}} are positive. Taking the corresponding operator block of (60) and cancelling g𝒏​g𝒏′\sqrt{g_{\bm{n}}g_{\bm{n}^{\prime}}} gives

⟨𝒏|ωX​K|𝒏′⟩=⟨𝒏|ωX|𝒏′⟩​ωK1.\langle\bm{n}|\omega_{XK}|\bm{n}^{\prime}\rangle=\langle\bm{n}|\omega_{X}|\bm{n}^{\prime}\rangle\,\omega_{K}^{1}.

Remark 7.

The filter G1/2G^{1/2} is injective, although its inverse is unbounded. The number-basis argument above uses only its positive eigenvalues; it does not apply the inverse to a trace-class operator. This distinction is useful when seeking quantitative versions of (59). We also note why the standard equality condition for data processing does not suffice here. By Petz’s theorem [31, 32], equality in (55) implies that ωX​K\omega_{XK} is recovered from ζY​K\zeta_{YK} by a local channel on YY; since Φ\Phi is entanglement breaking, this only shows that ωX​K\omega_{XK} is separable, whereas the instrument argument yields a product.

3.4 From equality to independent outputs

Proof of (i)⇒\Rightarrow(ii) in Theorem 1.

Let ωC​E=Uη​(ρA⊗ρB)​Uη†\omega_{CE}=U_{\eta}(\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B})U_{\eta}^{\dagger} and assume Lη​(A,B)=0L_{\eta}(A,B)=0.

1. Add a thermal equality pair.

In Lemma 3, set

(ρA1,ρB1)=(ρA,ρB),(ρA2,ρB2)=(τ2,τ2).(\rho_{A_{1}},\rho_{B_{1}})=(\rho_{A},\rho_{B}),\qquad(\rho_{A_{2}},\rho_{B_{2}})=(\tau_{2},\tau_{2}). (61)

All four inputs are independent. If the original energies are 𝖤A,𝖤B\mathsf{E}_{A},\mathsf{E}_{B}, the total energy in this circuit is 𝖤A+𝖤B+4​m\mathsf{E}_{A}+\mathsf{E}_{B}+4m. Every beam splitter preserves that total, so the energy bound (9) makes all circuit entropies finite. The auxiliary state has the form

(τ2)A2⊗(τ2)B2=3−2​m​exp⁡[−log⁡(3/2)​(HA2+HB2)].(\tau_{2})_{A_{2}}\otimes(\tau_{2})_{B_{2}}=3^{-2m}\exp[-\log(3/2)(H_{A_{2}}+H_{B_{2}})].

Uη​(τ2⊗τ2)​Uη†=(τ2)GC⊗(τ2)GE.U_{\eta}(\tau_{2}\otimes\tau_{2})U_{\eta}^{\dagger}=(\tau_{2})_{G_{C}}\otimes(\tau_{2})_{G_{E}}. (62)

In particular, the auxiliary outputs are independent and Lη​(A2,B2)=m​g​(2)−η​m​g​(2)−(1−η)​m​g​(2)=0L_{\eta}(A_{2},B_{2})=mg(2)-\eta mg(2)-(1-\eta)mg(2)=0.

2. Apply the doubling identity.

Use the first circuit order in Fig. 1(a), with M=A+​B+M=A_{+}B_{+}. Lemma 3, at p=ηp=\eta, gives

0=Lη​(A+,B+)+Lη​(A−,B−∣M)+I​(C−;E+∣C+)Ξ.0=L_{\eta}(A_{+},B_{+})+L_{\eta}(A_{-},B_{-}\mid M)+I(C_{-};E_{+}\mid C_{+})_{\Xi}. (63)

The lemma verifies the conditional-independence hypothesis needed for the conditional deficit. All three terms are nonnegative, hence

I​(C−;E+∣C+)Ξ=0.I(C_{-};E_{+}\mid C_{+})_{\Xi}=0. (64)
3. Read the circuit as local thermal noise.

By the commutation of the two kinds of beam splitters proved in Lemma 3, the second circuit order has the same four-output state Ξ\Xi. Immediately after the η\eta-beam splitters, the state is

ωC​E⊗(τ2)GC⊗(τ2)GE.\omega_{CE}\otimes(\tau_{2})_{G_{C}}\otimes(\tau_{2})_{G_{E}}. (65)

Mix E,GEE,G_{E} on the balanced beam splitter and retain J:=E+J:=E_{+}. The state before mixing C,GCC,G_{C} is

σC​J⊗(τ2)GC,σC​J=(idC⊗Φ)​(ωC​E).\sigma_{CJ}\otimes(\tau_{2})_{G_{C}},\qquad\sigma_{CJ}=(\operatorname{id}_{C}\otimes\Phi)(\omega_{CE}). (66)

3.5 Gaussian characterization and the converse

Equation (5) already gives (ii)⇒\Rightarrow(i), because its two deficits are nonnegative.

Proof of (ii)⇒\Rightarrow(iii).

The finite-energy quantum Darmois–Skitovich characterization, Proposition 14, applies to the independent inputs and product outputs. It gives Gaussianity and equality of covariance matrices. Appendix B gives the full proof by reducing each quadrature direction to two independent scalar random variables. Their orthogonal mixtures are independent, which forces Gaussian laws with equal variances. The means remain unrestricted. ∎

Proof of (iii)⇒\Rightarrow(i), including product outputs.

Finite energy controls the circuit entropies and the scalar quadrature variances. The restriction 0<η<10<\eta<1 ensures that both mixing coefficients are nonzero. At either endpoint, arbitrary inputs already have zero linear deficit.

An immediate consequence concerns optimization at fixed covariance.

Corollary 9 (Uniqueness at fixed covariance).

Fix a physical covariance matrix VV and 0<η<10<\eta<1. Proof.

The qEPI makes the deficit nonnegative. Theorem 1 and uniqueness of a Gaussian state with prescribed mean and covariance identify its zero set. ∎

4 Equality in the exponential qEPI

The exponential inequality itself is established: the balanced case is [1, Theorem VII.2, Eq. (89)], and arbitrary transmissivity is [3, Eq. (5)]. We derive its equality characterization from Theorem 1.

The proof has two distinct steps. We first propagate zero affine deficit to a Gaussian limit. We then use strictness within the Gaussian family to recover linear equality for the original inputs.

4.1 The fixed affine weight

Unlike classical differential entropy, bosonic entropy has no scaling rule that converts a change of quadrature scale into an additive entropy constant. One should therefore distinguish the single linear inequality (2) from the full affine family equivalent to (3). We use that family explicitly when treating exponential equality.

The equivalence between the complete affine family and exponential qEPI is the variational reformulation used in [17, Eqs. (106), (107), (115)]. The following relative-entropy identity spells out the elementary algebra and its equality condition. Set

𝒵η\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}_{\eta} =η​eS⁡(A)/m+(1−η)​eS⁡(B)/m,\displaystyle=\eta e^{S(A)/m}+(1-\eta)e^{S(B)/m},
δ\displaystyle\delta =S⁡(C)−m​log⁡𝒵η,p∗=η​eS⁡(A)/m𝒵η.\displaystyle=S(C)-m\log\mathcal{Z}_{\eta},\qquad p_{*}=\frac{\eta e^{S(A)/m}}{\mathcal{Z}_{\eta}}. (73)

The finite input entropies ensure 𝒵η>0\mathcal{Z}_{\eta}>0 and p∗∈(0,1)p_{*}\in(0,1). For a direct expansion, observe

log⁡p∗\displaystyle\log p_{*} =log⁡η+S⁡(A)/m−log⁡𝒵η,\displaystyle=\log\eta+S(A)/m-\log\mathcal{Z}_{\eta},
log⁡(1−p∗)\displaystyle\log(1-p_{*}) =log⁡(1−η)+S⁡(B)/m−log⁡𝒵η.\displaystyle=\log(1-\eta)+S(B)/m-\log\mathcal{Z}_{\eta}. (74)

Substitution into (19) gives

md(p∥p∗)=md(p∥η)−pS(A)−(1−p)S(B)+mlog𝒵η.md(p\|p_{*})=md(p\|\eta)-pS(A)-(1-p)S(B)+m\log\mathcal{Z}_{\eta}. (75)

Adding δ=S⁡(C)−m​log⁡𝒵η\delta=S(C)-m\log\mathcal{Z}_{\eta} proves

Fp(A,B)=δ+md(p∥p∗).F_{p}(A,B)=\delta+m\,d(p\|p_{*}). (76)

Thus exponential equality is Fp∗=0F_{p_{*}}=0. Ordinary linear equality is Fη=0F_{\eta}=0. Given the established qEPI, (76) implies

Lη=0⟺δ=0andS(A)=S(B).L_{\eta}=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\delta=0\ \text{and}\ S(A)=S(B). (77)

The affine inequalities for all pp together are equivalent to the exponential qEPI; the single case p=ηp=\eta is the linear qEPI.

4.2 Strict Gaussian entropy-power concavity

Gaussian entropy is an average of log determinants over x∈(−1/2,1/2)x\in(-1/2,1/2). This representation allows Minkowski’s determinant inequality to be applied pointwise. The entropy formula follows from [21, Eq. (3.27)]; the determinant inequality and its equality case are recalled in Appendix A.5. The following Gaussian equality characterization can also be deduced from the EPnI for Gaussian states [33, Appendix A.8], combined with the strict concavity of N↦eg⁡(N)N\mapsto e^{g(N)} and of V↦S⁡(γV)V\mapsto S(\gamma_{V}). We include a direct proof based on a log-determinant representation of Gaussian entropy.

Lemma 10.

Let VA,VBV_{A},V_{B} be covariance matrices satisfying V+i​Ω/2≥0V+i\Omega/2\geq 0, and let p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1] and 0<η<10<\eta<1. Then

Fp(γVA,γVB)=0⟺VA=VBandp=η.F_{p}(\gamma_{V_{A}},\gamma_{V_{B}})=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad V_{A}=V_{B}\ \text{and}\ p=\eta. (78)
Proof.

Recall gg from (9), including g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0. Williamson decomposition (13) gives

S(γV)=m+12∫−1/21/2logdet(V+ixΩ)dx.S(\gamma_{V})=m+\frac{1}{2}\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\log\det(V+ix\Omega)\,\mathrm{d}x. (79)

Indeed, V+i​x​Ω=𝖲⁡(diag⁡(ν1,ν1,…)+i​x​Ω)​𝖲TV+ix\Omega=\mathsf{S}(\operatorname{diag}(\nu_{1},\nu_{1},\ldots)+ix\Omega)\mathsf{S}^{T}. Since (det𝖲)2=1(\det\mathsf{S})^{2}=1, the determinant equals ∏j=1m(νj2−x2)\prod_{j=1}^{m}(\nu_{j}^{2}-x^{2}). For each ν≥1/2\nu\geq 1/2, split log⁡(ν2−x2)=log⁡(ν−x)+log⁡(ν+x)\log(\nu^{2}-x^{2})=\log(\nu-x)+\log(\nu+x) and integrate:

1+12∫−1/21/2log(ν2−x2)dx=g(ν−1/2).1+\frac{1}{2}\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\log(\nu^{2}-x^{2})\,\mathrm{d}x=g(\nu-1/2). (80)

The left side equals 1+∫−1/21/2log(ν+x)dx=(ν+1/2)log(ν+1/2)−(ν−1/2)log(ν−1/2)1+\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\log(\nu+x)\mathrm{d}x=(\nu+1/2)\log(\nu+1/2)-(\nu-1/2)\log(\nu-1/2). This is g⁡(ν−1/2)g(\nu-1/2). Endpoint integrals are improper when ν=1/2\nu=1/2, but their logarithmic singularities are integrable. Summing and using (14) proves (79).

For |x|<1/2|x|<1/2, V+i​x​ΩV+ix\Omega is positive definite Hermitian. One way to see this is to write it as a convex combination of V+i​Ω/2V+i\Omega/2 and V−i​Ω/2V-i\Omega/2 with strictly positive coefficients; their kernels cannot intersect because their sum is 2​V>02V>0. Let

fV​(x)\displaystyle f_{V}(x) =det(V+i​x​Ω)1/(2​m),\displaystyle=\det(V+ix\Omega)^{1/(2m)},
𝒢⁡(f)\displaystyle\mathcal{G}(f) =exp(∫−1/21/2logf(x)dx).\displaystyle=\exp\left(\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\log f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\right). (81)

Minkowski’s determinant inequality [34] is strict for positive definite matrices unless they are positively proportional. Apply this result pointwise to the positive Hermitian matrices VA+i​x​ΩV_{A}+ix\Omega and VB+i​x​ΩV_{B}+ix\Omega. It gives

fη​VA+(1−η)​VB​(x)≥η​fVA​(x)+(1−η)​fVB​(x).f_{\eta V_{A}+(1-\eta)V_{B}}(x)\geq\eta f_{V_{A}}(x)+(1-\eta)f_{V_{B}}(x). (82)

Its equality condition for positive definite matrices is positive proportionality. We next use concavity of the integral geometric mean. If a=𝒢⁡(f)>0a=\mathcal{G}(f)>0, b=𝒢⁡(h)>0b=\mathcal{G}(h)>0, and r=η​a/(η​a+(1−η)​b)r=\eta a/(\eta a+(1-\eta)b), then

4.3 Quantum convolution and the finite-energy limit

Only the following standard limit statements are needed: the trace-norm quantum CLT [19, Theorem 5] and entropy continuity under an oscillator energy bound [20, Lemma 15]. We verify their hypotheses for the present iterates below.

The nn-fold quantum convolution.

For an mm-mode state ρ\rho and an integer n≥1n\geq 1, take nn independent copies of ρ\rho. Apply a passive unitary whose first output quadrature vector is

Rout,1=1n​∑j=1nRj,R_{\mathrm{out},1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}R_{j}, (85)

and discard the other outputs. Here RjR_{j} is the 2​m2m-component quadrature vector on copy jj. Such a unitary exists: complete the unit vector n−1/2(1,…,1)n^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1) to a real orthogonal matrix on the copy index and apply this matrix to every quadrature component. The resulting matrix is both orthogonal and symplectic. Denote the retained state by ρ⊞n\rho^{\boxplus n}, and put ρ⊞1=ρ\rho^{\boxplus 1}=\rho. Independence of the inputs and commutation of observables on distinct copies give

χρ⊞n​(ξ)=χρ​(ξ/n)n,ξ∈ℝ2​m.\chi_{\rho^{\boxplus n}}(\xi)=\chi_{\rho}(\xi/\sqrt{n})^{n},\qquad\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2m}. (86)

This also shows that the retained state is independent of the chosen orthogonal completion. The state ρ⊞n\rho^{\boxplus n} is the nn-fold symmetric quantum convolution of ρ\rho studied in [19, 23, 27]; the characteristic function (86) shows that it coincides with the nn-fold convolution defined there. For n=2n=2 it is ℬ1/2​(ρ⊗ρ)\mathcal{B}_{1/2}(\rho\otimes\rho), and repeated balanced self-convolution gives ρ⊞2k\rho^{\boxplus 2^{k}} after kk steps.

If ρ\rho has displacement dd and covariance VV, then ρ⊞n\rho^{\boxplus n} has displacement n​d\sqrt{n}\,d and covariance VV. In particular, for a centered state, all these convolutions have the same oscillator energy

𝖤=Tr⁡ρ​Hm=tr⁡V−m2.\mathsf{E}=\operatorname{Tr}\rho H_{m}=\frac{\operatorname{tr}V-m}{2}. (87)

This is why centering precedes the limit argument.

Winter’s Lemma 15 [20] yields the explicit bound

|S⁡(ρ)−S⁡(σ)|≤2​ϵ​m​g​(𝖤m​ϵ)+h2​(ϵ),|S(\rho)-S(\sigma)|\leq 2\epsilon m\,g\!\left(\frac{\mathsf{E}}{m\epsilon}\right)+h_{2}(\epsilon), (88)

where ϵ=12​‖ρ−σ‖1∈(0,1]\epsilon=\tfrac{1}{2}\left\lVert\rho-\sigma\right\rVert_{1}\in(0,1] and both oscillator energies are at most 𝖤\mathsf{E}. Here h2​(t)=−t​log⁡t−(1−t)​log⁡(1−t)h_{2}(t)=-t\log t-(1-t)\log(1-t). The right side tends to zero with ϵ\epsilon. The following lemmas record the precise continuity and limit statements.

Lemma 11 (Entropy continuity under an oscillator energy bound).

Let ωj\omega_{j} and ω\omega be mm-mode states such that

‖ωj−ω‖1⟶0,max⁡{Tr⁡ωj​Hm,Tr⁡ω​Hm}≤𝖤<∞.\left\lVert\omega_{j}-\omega\right\rVert_{1}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad\max\{\operatorname{Tr}\omega_{j}H_{m},\operatorname{Tr}\omega H_{m}\}\leq\mathsf{E}<\infty.

Then S⁡(ωj)→S⁡(ω)S(\omega_{j})\to S(\omega).

Proof.

It follows directly from (88). ∎

Lemma 12 (Finite-energy convolution central limit theorem).

Let ρ\rho be a centered mm-mode state of finite energy and covariance VV. Let γV\gamma_{V} be the centered Gaussian state with covariance VV. Then

‖ρ⊞n−γV‖1⟶0,S⁡(ρ⊞n)⟶S⁡(γV).\left\lVert\rho^{\boxplus n}-\gamma_{V}\right\rVert_{1}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad S(\rho^{\boxplus n})\longrightarrow S(\gamma_{V}). (89)
Proof.

The finite-energy assumption gives all second moments. The trace-norm convergence is the Cushen–Hudson theorem in the form of [19, Theorem 5]; quantitative rates under higher moments are given in [19, 23]. Centering and (87) keep every iterate, and its Gaussian limit, in the same energy ball. Then Lemma 11 gives the desired entropy convergence. ∎

4.4 Proof of Theorem 2

Proof of Theorem 2.

Different displacements of the inputs do not alter any entropy, hence we can assume the displacements are all 00. Fix p=p∗p=p_{*} from the original centered pair. Exponential equality means Fp​(A,B)=0F_{p}(A,B)=0. For X=A,B,CX=A,B,C and each integer k≥0k\geq 0, let ρX(k)=ρX⊞2k\rho_{X}^{(k)}=\rho_{X}^{\boxplus 2^{k}}. Apply Lemma 3 to two independent copies of (ρA(k),ρB(k))(\rho_{A}^{(k)},\rho_{B}^{(k)}). Its plus pair is the next iterate, so

0≤Fp​(A(k+1),B(k+1))≤2​Fp​(A(k),B(k)).0\leq F_{p}(A^{(k+1)},B^{(k+1)})\leq 2F_{p}(A^{(k)},B^{(k)}). (90)

The discarded terms are the conditional deficit and a CMI. The conditional qEPI is used at this fixed p=p∗p=p_{*}, which need not yet equal η\eta. Since the initial deficit is zero, induction gives

Fp​(A(k),B(k))=0(k≥0).F_{p}(A^{(k)},B^{(k)})=0\qquad(k\geq 0). (91)

That the output of the iterated pair is ρC(k)\rho_{C}^{(k)} follows from commutation of the two kinds of mixing. The same pp is retained for all kk.

For each X=A,B,CX=A,B,C, the definition of the nn-fold convolution and independence give dX(k)=0d_{X^{(k)}}=0 and VX(k)=VXV_{X^{(k)}}=V_{X}. Here VC=η​VA+(1−η)​VBV_{C}=\eta V_{A}+(1-\eta)V_{B} is fixed as well. By (8), each of the three sequences has its own fixed finite energy. Lemma 12 therefore gives trace-norm convergence to γVA\gamma_{V_{A}}, γVB\gamma_{V_{B}}, and γVC\gamma_{V_{C}}, respectively, and Lemma 11 gives convergence of all three entropies. The coefficient pp and the constant md(p∥η)md(p\|\eta) remain unchanged. We may consequently take the limit in the three finite entropy terms of (91), obtaining

Fp​(γVA,γVB)=0.F_{p}(\gamma_{V_{A}},\gamma_{V_{B}})=0. (92)

Lemma 10 yields VA=VBV_{A}=V_{B} and p=p∗=ηp=p_{*}=\eta. The formula for p∗p_{*} then gives S⁡(A)=S⁡(B)S(A)=S(B), and Lη​(A,B)=Fη​(A,B)=0L_{\eta}(A,B)=F_{\eta}(A,B)=0. Theorem 1 proves Gaussianity.

Conversely, matched-covariance Gaussian inputs have S⁡(C)=S⁡(A)=S⁡(B)S(C)=S(A)=S(B) and satisfy exponential equality directly. ∎

5 Discussion

The equality condition for the bosonic qEPI can be expressed entirely in terms of the two output systems: an independent finite-energy pair attains either entropy inequality precisely when its beam-splitter outputs are independent. The Gaussian characterization then follows from the quantum Darmois–Skitovich theorem. The thermal auxiliary is what connects an entropy condition on one output to this structural condition on both outputs.

The method also separates two roles of Gaussian states. The auxiliary thermal states are introduced at a fixed finite energy to obtain strict information loss. The Gaussian limit in the exponential proof serves a different purpose: it determines the affine weight and the input covariances. The linear equality proof is complete before that limit argument is used.

A natural extension of the present work is a quantitative version of the qEPI: when the deficit is small, the input states should be close to Gaussian states with nearly equal covariance matrices. The classical counterpart is treated in [35], and stability of the quantum Darmois–Skitovich theorem is treated in [8]. This quantitative version would have to control the information lost in the vacuum branch and the removal of thermal noise. In the present proof, the effect GG has eigenvalues tending to zero, and the inverse characteristic multiplier is unbounded. Exact injectivity therefore does not itself give a stability estimate. Energy-dependent estimates are a natural next question.

Appendix A Auxiliary operator calculations

A.1 Moments and characteristic functions

The products in (7) are quadratic-form expectations. Equivalently, (Vρ)j​k(V_{\rho})_{jk} is the real part of the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product between (Rj−(dρ)j​I)​ρ1/2(R_{j}-(d_{\rho})_{j}I)\rho^{1/2} and (Rk−(dρ)k​I)​ρ1/2(R_{k}-(d_{\rho})_{k}I)\rho^{1/2}. Their squared Hilbert–Schmidt norms are finite under the second-moment assumption. This also justifies the second moment of every scalar quadrature ξT​R\xi^{T}R.

The Weyl representation is irreducible, so its linear span is ultraweakly dense in the bounded operators. A trace-class operator whose expectation against every Weyl operator vanishes is therefore zero. This proves the uniqueness of characteristic functions used in the main text.

A.2 Oscillator entropy bound

For β>0\beta>0, nonnegativity of relative entropy to the Gibbs state gives

S⁡(ρ)≤β​Tr⁡ρ​Hm−m​log⁡(1−e−β).S(\rho)\leq\beta\operatorname{Tr}\rho H_{m}-m\log(1-e^{-\beta}).

Minimizing over β\beta yields (9). For zero energy the state is the vacuum. Nonnegativity of the mode number operators bounds each subsystem energy by the total energy.

A.3 The heterodyne Fourier identity

We verify (42). Define the bounded operator

T⁡(w)=∫ℂmew⋅z¯−w¯⋅z​Mhet​(𝑑z)T(w)=\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}e^{w\cdot\bar{z}-\bar{w}\cdot z}M_{\rm het}(\mathrm{d}z) (93)

as a weak integral, meaning equality after taking matrix elements; its integrand is a bounded scalar function against a POVM. The complex Gaussian integral ∫ℂmπ−m​e−|z|2+A⋅z+B⋅z¯​d2​m​z=eA⋅B\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}\pi^{-m}e^{-|z|^{2}+A\cdot z+B\cdot\bar{z}}\mathrm{d}^{2m}z=e^{A\cdot B}, for A,B∈ℂmA,B\in\mathbb{C}^{m}, gives

⟨u|T⁡(w)|v⟩=⟨u|v⟩​eu¯⋅w−w¯⋅v−|w|2.\langle u|T(w)|v\rangle=\langle u|v\rangle e^{\bar{u}\cdot w-\bar{w}\cdot v-|w|^{2}}. (94)

Normal ordering, 𝒟(w)=e−|w|2/2e∑jwj​aj†e−∑jw¯jaj\mathcal{D}(w)=e^{-|w|^{2}/2}e^{\sum_{j}w_{j}a_{j}^{\dagger}}e^{-\sum_{j}\bar{w}_{j}a_{j}}, shows that this is the matrix element of e−|w|2/2𝒟(w)e^{-|w|^{2}/2}\mathcal{D}(w). Coherent vectors span a dense subspace, so the two bounded operators are equal. Taking their expectation in ρ\rho proves (42).

The integral in (41) is a Bochner integral, meaning a norm limit of integrals of simple trace-class-valued functions. Its integrand is trace-norm measurable and has norm Qρ​(z)Q_{\rho}(z), an integrable probability density. This establishes existence in trace norm.

A.4 Integral maps and finite instrument entropies

For complete positivity of the maps in (51), it suffices to check every finite-dimensional auxiliary system R0R_{0}. If TX​R0≥0T_{XR_{0}}\geq 0 is trace class, its heterodyne operator density is

AR0​(z)=π−m​(⟨z|⊗I)​TX​R0​(|z⟩⊗I)≥0.A_{R_{0}}(z)=\pi^{-m}(\langle z|\otimes I)T_{XR_{0}}(|z\rangle\otimes I)\geq 0.

Writing Bz=πz−c⁡(z)​|0⟩​⟨0|≥0B_{z}=\pi_{z}-c(z)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|\geq 0, the amplified residual map is

(Λ0⊗idR0)​(T)=∫ℂmBz⊗AR0​(z)​d2​m​z≥0.(\Lambda_{0}\otimes\operatorname{id}_{R_{0}})(T)=\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}B_{z}\otimes A_{R_{0}}(z)\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z\geq 0.

The integral exists in trace norm: the integrand is measurable and

∫Tr⁡Bz​Tr​AR0​(z)​d2​m​z≤∫Tr⁡AR0​(z)​d2​m​z=Tr⁡T.\int\operatorname{Tr}B_{z}\,\operatorname{Tr}A_{R_{0}}(z)\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z\leq\int\operatorname{Tr}A_{R_{0}}(z)\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z=\operatorname{Tr}T.

It therefore defines a bounded completely positive map on trace-class operators. The same argument applies to Λ1\Lambda_{1} and their sum. Only ordinary quantum channels on separable Hilbert spaces are used in the data-processing steps [25, Theorem 1].

We now justify the entropy chain rules in Proposition 6, using its notation. Both MfM_{f} commute with HmH_{m} and satisfy Mf2≤IM_{f}^{2}\leq I, so

pf​Tr⁡(Hm​ωX′f)≤Tr⁡(Hm​ωX)<∞.p_{f}\operatorname{Tr}(H_{m}\omega^{f}_{X^{\prime}})\leq\operatorname{Tr}(H_{m}\omega_{X})<\infty.

The Gibbs bound makes each S⁡(ωX′f)S(\omega^{f}_{X^{\prime}}) finite. The unflagged output has energy Tr⁡(Hm​ζY)=12​Tr⁡(Hm​ωX)+m\operatorname{Tr}(H_{m}\zeta_{Y})=\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(H_{m}\omega_{X})+m. Since ζY=∑fpf​ζYf\zeta_{Y}=\sum_{f}p_{f}\zeta_{Y}^{f}, each output branch has finite energy and hence finite entropy as well. Finally, ωK=∑fpf​ωKf\omega_{K}=\sum_{f}p_{f}\omega_{K}^{f} and entropy concavity imply ∑fpf​S​(ωKf)≤S⁡(ωK)<∞\sum_{f}p_{f}S(\omega_{K}^{f})\leq S(\omega_{K})<\infty. Subadditivity then gives finite entropy for every joint state in Proposition 6, including the states with the finite flag.

A.5 Minkowski’s determinant inequality

For reference, we give the positive-definite Hermitian case of Minkowski’s determinant inequality [34], including equality. Let H,KH,K be positive definite Hermitian matrices of size d=2​md=2m and 0<t<10<t<1. Let λ1,…,λd>0\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d}>0 be the eigenvalues of H−1/2KH−1/2H^{-1/2}KH^{-1/2}. Set e0​(λ)=1e_{0}(\lambda)=1; for 1≤k≤d1\leq k\leq d let ek​(λ)e_{k}(\lambda) be the sum of all products of kk distinct eigenvalues. Arithmetic–geometric mean over those products gives

ek​(λ)≥(dk)​(∏j=1dλj)k/d.e_{k}(\lambda)\geq\binom{d}{k}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{d}\lambda_{j}\right)^{k/d}. (95)

Each eigenvalue occurs in (d−1k−1)\binom{d-1}{k-1} products, which explains the exponent k/dk/d. Expanding the product and applying these inequalities yields

∏j=1d[(1−t)+t​λj]\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^{d}[(1-t)+t\lambda_{j}] =∑k=0d(1−t)d−k​tk​ek​(λ)\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{d}(1-t)^{d-k}t^{k}e_{k}(\lambda)
≥[(1−t)+t​(∏jλj)1/d]d.\displaystyle\geq\left[(1-t)+t\left(\prod_{j}\lambda_{j}\right)^{1/d}\right]^{d}. (96)

Multiplication by detH\det H proves

det((1−t)​H+t​K)1/d≥(1−t)​det(H)1/d+t​det(K)1/d.\det((1-t)H+tK)^{1/d}\geq(1-t)\det(H)^{1/d}+t\det(K)^{1/d}. (97)

If equality holds, the k=1k=1 arithmetic–geometric mean equality forces all λj\lambda_{j} to be equal (all expansion coefficients are positive). Equivalently K=c​HK=cH for a positive scalar cc; this also suffices for equality.

Appendix B Gaussian characterization from independent outputs

The characterization in Proposition 14 is established: it is the finite-energy instance of Cuesta’s quantum Darmois–Skitovich theorem [8, Theorem 7, Corollary 8]. The one-mode predecessor is [9, Sec. III]. We retain the proof for completeness; the reduction to one-dimensional quadrature laws follows the same principle as Cuesta’s proof. The scalar argument is stated first, followed by its application to quadrature laws.

The scalar statement is the two-variable finite-variance specialization of the classical Darmois–Skitovich theorem [36, 37]; see [38] for the general statement and its history. The finite-variance proof below is the standard one based on the second derivatives of the logarithms of the characteristic functions. Equality of the variances follows also from the zero covariance of the orthogonal output forms.

Lemma 13 (Scalar finite-variance Darmois–Skitovich lemma).

Let X,YX,Y be independent real random variables with finite second moments. Let a,b>0a,b>0 satisfy a2+b2=1a^{2}+b^{2}=1. If a​X+b​YaX+bY and −b​X+a​Y-bX+aY are independent, then X,YX,Y are Gaussian with the same variance, allowing distinct means. Variance zero is permitted and means a constant random variable.

Proof.

Let φ⁡(t)=𝔼​ei​t​X\varphi(t)=\mathbb{E}e^{itX} and ψ⁡(t)=𝔼​ei​t​Y\psi(t)=\mathbb{E}e^{itY}. The two independence assumptions give, for every s,t∈ℝs,t\in\mathbb{R},

φ⁡(a​s−b​t)​ψ​(b​s+a​t)=φ⁡(a​s)​ψ​(b​s)​φ​(−b​t)​ψ​(a​t).\varphi(as-bt)\psi(bs+at)=\varphi(as)\psi(bs)\varphi(-bt)\psi(at). (98)

The left side is the joint characteristic function of the output linear forms; the right side is the product of their marginals.

Finite second moments justify two differentiations under the expectation: φ′​(t)=i​𝔼​[X​ei​t​X]\varphi^{\prime}(t)=i\mathbb{E}[Xe^{itX}] and φ′′​(t)=−𝔼⁡[X2​ei​t​X]\varphi^{\prime\prime}(t)=-\mathbb{E}[X^{2}e^{itX}], continuously in tt, and similarly for ψ\psi. Since both characteristic functions equal one at zero, they are nonzero on a small interval. There choose twice continuously differentiable logarithms ℓX=log⁡φ\ell_{X}=\log\varphi, ℓY=log⁡ψ\ell_{Y}=\log\psi with ℓX​(0)=ℓY​(0)=0\ell_{X}(0)=\ell_{Y}(0)=0. On a sufficiently small connected neighborhood of (0,0)(0,0) the logarithm of (98) is an exact additive identity: its two sides can differ only by a continuous 2​π​i​ℤ2\pi i\mathbb{Z}-valued function, which vanishes at the origin and therefore throughout that neighborhood.

Differentiate that identity first in ss and then in tt. Terms depending only on ss or only on tt drop out, giving

−a​b​ℓX′′​(a​s−b​t)+a​b​ℓY′′​(b​s+a​t)=0.-ab\ell_{X}^{\prime\prime}(as-bt)+ab\ell_{Y}^{\prime\prime}(bs+at)=0. (99)

The map (s,t)↦(u,v)=(a​s−b​t,b​s+a​t)(s,t)\mapsto(u,v)=(as-bt,bs+at) is invertible and maps an open neighborhood of the origin onto another such neighborhood. There is therefore r>0r>0 such that ℓX′′​(u)=ℓY′′​(v)\ell_{X}^{\prime\prime}(u)=\ell_{Y}^{\prime\prime}(v) whenever |u|,|v|<r|u|,|v|<r. Taking v=0v=0, then u=0u=0, shows that both second derivatives are constant. At zero they equal minus the respective variances, so Var⁡X=Var⁡Y=:σ2\operatorname{Var}X=\operatorname{Var}Y=:\sigma^{2}. Integration gives

φ(u)=ei​x¯​u−σ2​u2/2,ψ(u)=ei​y¯​u−σ2​u2/2(|u|<r),\varphi(u)=e^{i\bar{x}u-\sigma^{2}u^{2}/2},\qquad\psi(u)=e^{i\bar{y}u-\sigma^{2}u^{2}/2}\quad(|u|<r), (100)

where x¯=𝔼​X\bar{x}=\mathbb{E}X and y¯=𝔼​Y\bar{y}=\mathbb{E}Y.

Local agreement of characteristic functions is not enough by itself. To extend it, substitute (s,t)=(a​u,−b​u)(s,t)=(au,-bu) and (b​u,a​u)(bu,au) into the original global identity (98). Using φ⁡(−v)=φ⁡(v)¯\varphi(-v)=\overline{\varphi(v)} and the analogous identity for ψ\psi yields the exact recursions

φ⁡(u)\displaystyle\varphi(u) =φ⁡(a2​u)​φ​(b2​u)​|ψ⁡(a​b​u)|2,\displaystyle=\varphi(a^{2}u)\varphi(b^{2}u)|\psi(abu)|^{2},
ψ⁡(u)\displaystyle\psi(u) =ψ⁡(a2​u)​ψ​(b2​u)​|φ⁡(a​b​u)|2.\displaystyle=\psi(a^{2}u)\psi(b^{2}u)|\varphi(abu)|^{2}. (101)

Every argument on the right has absolute value at most q​|u|q|u|, where q=max⁡{a2,b2,a​b}<1q=\max\{a^{2},b^{2},ab\}<1. If the Gaussian formulas hold on [−R,R][-R,R], these recursions prove them on [−R/q,R/q][-R/q,R/q]: the mean coefficient is a2+b2=1a^{2}+b^{2}=1 and the variance coefficient is a4+b4+2​a2​b2=1a^{4}+b^{4}+2a^{2}b^{2}=1. Start with any 0<R<r0<R<r and iterate. The intervals [−R/qn,R/qn][-R/q^{n},R/q^{n}] exhaust the real line, so both formulas hold globally. The uniqueness theorem for classical characteristic functions identifies the two laws as the stated Gaussians. ∎

Proposition 14 (Finite-energy quantum characterization).

If independent finite-energy mm-mode inputs have independent outputs under a beam splitter with 0<η<10<\eta<1, they are Gaussian with equal covariance matrices and arbitrary displacement vectors.

Proof.

Fix any real vector ξ∈ℝ2​m\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2m}. The self-adjoint quadrature ξT​RA\xi^{T}R_{A} has a classical spectral law in state ρA\rho_{A}: its probability of a Borel set B⊆ℝB\subseteq\mathbb{R} is Tr⁡ρA​𝟏B​(ξT​RA)\operatorname{Tr}\rho_{A}\mathbf{1}_{B}(\xi^{T}R_{A}), where 𝟏B​(ξT​RA)\mathbf{1}_{B}(\xi^{T}R_{A}) is its spectral projection. Let XX have this law, and let YY have the corresponding law for ξT​RB\xi^{T}R_{B}. Their joint law in the product input is the independent product of these two laws. Both second moments are finite; this follows from the quadratic-form interpretation of (7) and Tr⁡ρ​Rj2<∞\operatorname{Tr}\rho R_{j}^{2}<\infty.

The two operators ξT​RA\xi^{T}R_{A} and ξT​RB\xi^{T}R_{B} act on different tensor factors, so their spectral measures commute. Their two linear combinations therefore have the ordinary joint law of a​X+b​YaX+bY and −b​X+a​Y-bX+aY, where a=ηa=\sqrt{\eta}, b=1−ηb=\sqrt{1-\eta}. By (1), this is also the joint spectral law of ξT​RC\xi^{T}R_{C} and ξT​RE\xi^{T}R_{E} in the output state. Product outputs make these laws independent. Lemma 13 applies.

Thus, for each ξ\xi, XX is Gaussian with mean ξT​dA\xi^{T}d_{A} and variance ξT​VA​ξ\xi^{T}V_{A}\xi, and YY is Gaussian with mean ξT​dB\xi^{T}d_{B} and the same variance. Evaluating their scalar characteristic functions at one gives

χA​(ξ)=ei​ξT​dA−ξT​VA​ξ/2,χB​(ξ)=ei​ξT​dB−ξT​VB​ξ/2.\chi_{A}(\xi)=e^{i\xi^{T}d_{A}-\xi^{T}V_{A}\xi/2},\qquad\chi_{B}(\xi)=e^{i\xi^{T}d_{B}-\xi^{T}V_{B}\xi/2}. (102)

These hold for every ξ\xi, so the definition (12) proves Gaussianity. The equality ξT​(VA−VB)​ξ=0\xi^{T}(V_{A}-V_{B})\xi=0 for every real ξ\xi implies VA=VBV_{A}=V_{B} by polarization of real quadratic forms. This is the finite-energy instance of the exact quantum Darmois–Skitovich theorem [8, Theorem 7]. ∎
